name: Green
lede: Green is the color of leaves and grass, everywhere in nature yet hard for people to make or keep: for centuries an unstable color of youth, love, chance and poison, and today the color of nature itself.

sections.title: A word for growing
sections.body:
Green is the color of growing plants, and its Latin name says so [1]. *Viridis*, the ancestor of French *vert* and Italian *verde*, belongs to a family of words for vigor and growth, such as *virere*, to be green or flourish, and *vis*, strength [1]. A link to *ver*, spring, is tempting, but Pastoureau notes that the sound changes argue against it [28]. Greek was vaguer. Its *glaukos* and *chloros* wavered between green, grey, blue and yellow and suggested pale, weak color; only *prasinos*, leek-colored, became a firm word for strong green, from the third or second century BC [2].

Nineteenth-century scholars took the thin vocabulary as proof that the Greeks were blind to green and blue [2]. That idea is a myth. Greek painters used malachite, green earths and even artificial copper greens, so they plainly saw green and made it [2]. Other languages cut the spectrum elsewhere. The Hanunoo of the Philippines sort colors by fresh and dry as much as by hue, and English still has no settled word for the band between yellow and green [3][4]. Yet *green* is common: in modern written English it appears more than twice as often as *yellow* [5].

Scripture treats it sparingly. In the Bible green nearly always means grass and leaves, and the emerald is its only green gem [6]. In the Quran, of 33 mentions of the six basic colors, eight are green, and every one is good: plants, spring, paradise [7].

sections.title: Hard to make, harder to keep
sections.body:
Green is everywhere in nature, yet people learned to make it late. No Paleolithic cave painting uses green, though a green earth was available [8][9]. Ancient Egypt valued it: green meant fertility and rebirth, Osiris was painted with a green face, and the hieroglyph for green is a papyrus stalk [1]. Rome's painters handled it well. The painted garden in the Villa of Livia, of about 20 BC, uses green earths, malachite and artificial copper greens [10].

Every traditional green had a flaw. Malachite was costly and darkened, green earths covered weakly, plant greens faded, and copper greens corroded what lay near them [14]. Verdigris was made by hanging copper over vinegar, a method Theophrastus already describes, and it could eat holes in parchment [11][12]. A version mixed with resin, copper resinate, turns brown in light, which is why so many hills and trees in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italian paintings are now brown [13]. The verdigris itself may not deserve its bad name: modern tests show it darkens little [13]. Green earth, or [[terre-verte|terre verte]], is weak but permanent, and painters laid it under flesh; where the pink on top has faded, saints' faces now look green [9].

Painters did not simply mix blue and yellow. Pastoureau finds that practice common only in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and in the 1740s the painter Oudry attacked colleagues who mixed greens rather than buying green pigments [14]. Samuel van Hoogstraten complained in the 1670s that no green was good enough, and Velázquez never used a pure green at all [15].

Chemistry brought vivid greens and new dangers. Carl Scheele made a copper arsenite in 1775, and by 1858 about 100 square miles of British wallpaper were printed with [[scheele-s-green|Scheele's green]]; the death in 1861 of a 19-year-old artificial-flower maker, Matilda Scheurer, helped end its use [16][17]. [[emerald-green|Emerald green]], a copper aceto-arsenite found in 1814, was so poisonous it was sold as an insecticide [17][18]. The claim that arsenic from green wallpaper killed Napoleon is unproven: a 2008 study found his hair's arsenic high but steady across his whole life, though Pastoureau still treats it as possible [16][19]. The safe answer was [[viridian]], a chromium oxide made by the Parisian colorman Pannetier in 1838 and kept secret until Guignet's method of 1859; it became Cézanne's green [17].

sections.title: The forbidden mixture
sections.body:
Green is the one dye color that plants cannot give on their own, for all their greenness [21]. Dyers made it in two baths, first blue woad and then yellow weld, as in the English Lincoln and Kendal greens [22][23]. Medieval guilds made that hard. Blue dyers and yellow dyers held separate licenses, and in January 1386 the Nuremberg dyer Hans Töllner, licensed for blue and black, was found with yellow vats, fined, exiled to Augsburg and banned from his trade [23]. The two-bath method is old, but it was first described in print only in a Venetian dyeing manual of 1540 [23].

Even then green would not stay put. Late medieval French distinguished *vert gai*, a lively green, from *vert perdu*, a dimmed one, and a cloth could pass from the first to the second in weeks; green dyes kept badly until the eighteenth century [24]. In 1566 Henri Estienne observed that in France a man dressed in green seemed a little mad, while in Germany, where dyers ignored the bans, it signaled worth [23].

sections.title: Youth, love, chance and money
sections.body:
Roman moralists counted green among the showy, unreliable colors, and Romans thought it a barbarian taste [10][1]. Nero loved it, but the story that he watched gladiators through an emerald like sunglasses is disputed: Pastoureau reads the source as Nero resting his eyes on the stone, which was thought to soothe sight [10]. Rome's chariot teams ended with only two, the Blues and the Greens, and in Byzantium their rivalry boiled over in the Nika riots of 532, which left more than 30,000 dead [25].

The Church gave green a quiet role [26]. In 1195 the future Innocent III made it the liturgical color for ordinary days, a middle color between white, red and black, and it became the color priests wore most [26]. In Islam green rose from a dynastic color to a sacred one from the twelfth century [7]. Heraldry kept it rare: green never appears on more than 5 per cent of medieval coats of arms [27].

Medieval green meant youth and new love. On the first of May people had to wear something green, and young women of marriageable age wore it [28][29]. Pastoureau reads the green gown in van Eyck's Arnolfini portrait as a sign of hoped-for pregnancy, a reading others contest [29]. Hunters dressed in green, and so does the uncanny knight of *Sir Gawain and the Green Knight* [30]. From the mid-twelfth century devils could be green, and later witches were given green eyes [31][32].

Green also meant chance and money long before the dollar. In fourteenth-century northern Italy bankrupt debtors were put in the stocks in a green bonnet, and from the sixteenth century Venice covered its gaming tables in green cloth [24]. In the medieval list of sins green was avarice and yellow envy; Pastoureau thinks *green with envy* comes from language, while St Clair credits Shakespeare's *green-eyed monster* with fixing it [24][33].

Superstition grew around it. In 1673 Colbert ordered any ship with a green hull destroyed, since green was thought to attract lightning at sea [34]. The tale that Molière died on stage dressed in green is wrong: he was playing Argan, who wore no green, and the green ribbons belonged to another of his characters [35].

sections.title: Nature, safety and politics
sections.body:
Green came back with the pre-Romantics, for whom nature was a refuge [37]. Goethe found it soothing and hung his bedroom in Weimar in dark green [36]. On 12 July 1789 Camille Desmoulins pinned a green leaf to his hat as the first revolutionary cockade, but green was dropped before the Bastille fell on 14 July because it was the livery of the Count of Artois [37]. Napoleon did not start the fashion for Empire green, though he liked the color: it was fashionable before he took power and long after 1815 [19].

Green also became the signal for safety. Red for stop and green for go spread at sea and on the railways between about 1760 and 1840, when color theory made green red's partner; before that, green had been a color of disorder [38]. Green is now on 40 per cent of national flags [38]. *Khaki* comes from a Hindustani word for dust, adopted by British soldiers in India [39], and green settled into medicine, pharmacy and sport, from hospital walls to the Masters golf jacket, awarded since 1949 [40]. Ireland's green is younger than it looks: St Patrick's color was blue until the mid-1700s, and the name [[kelly-green|Kelly green]] appears only in the early 1900s [41].

Since the 1970s green has been the color of politics about the planet, and in 2001 eighty green parties signed a common charter in Canberra [42]. Polls in Europe put it second only to blue, chosen by 15 to 20 per cent of people, and under a tenth dislike it, often because they think it unlucky [42].

sections.title: The eye's middle color
sections.body:
Leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs red, orange, blue and violet light for photosynthesis and reflects the green, which is largely useless to the plant [43]. Many green birds have only yellow pigment in their feathers; the feather's structure adds the blue [49]. Gems take their green from traces of metal. An emerald is beryl colored by chromium, the same element that makes ruby red, and Colombian stones from mines opened in 1537 and 1567 define what most people now call emerald green [51][59]. Peridot was known as the evening emerald because its yellower green holds its glow at dusk [52]. Even weather paints it: the Statue of Liberty was brown copper in 1886 and had turned green by the early twentieth century [53].

Our eyes are tuned to the middle of the spectrum. They are most sensitive to yellow-green, which is why that stretch of a rainbow looks brightest, and in daylight blue light gives only a twentieth of the brightness response of the same amount of green [5][44]. At dusk the rods, most sensitive to green and blue-green, take over, so greens and blues hold their light while reds go dark [45]. Green and red are opposite ends of one channel in the visual system, which is why one can imagine a yellowish green but never a reddish green [46]. Early observers of afterimages noticed that the true partner of red is a blue-green, but the six-color wheel made plain green its accepted complement [47]. Blue and yellow paints make green because each absorbs most of the spectrum and both reflect a narrow band of green; blue and yellow light, added together, make white [48].

Look at a tree in sun. Leaves with light shining through them are an intense yellow-green, shaded leaves facing up turn blue-green from the sky, and the leaves lit from above are the lightest but the dullest, because their waxy surface reflects white light [50].

sections.title: Green in painting
sections.body:
Painters have long distrusted green. Gurney records the painter Asher Durand complaining around 1855 of the prejudice against it [5]. Kandinsky called pure green passive and bourgeois, like a fat cow, and Mondrian called it useless [57]. Painters learned to enliven it with its opposite: Pissarro, from the 1880s, framed a reddish sunset in green and a green spring scene in pink-red, and landscape painters still prime a canvas pink so that the warm ground shows through the greens [55][56]. Van Gogh wrote that in *[[art:commons-Q674846|The Night Café]]* he set red against green to express the terrible passions of humanity [54].

Green also confused critics. When Renoir painted green and purple patches on a nude's torso, a Paris critic compared her to a rotting corpse; Livingstone notes that Renoir was painting light reflected from leaves [58]. The trouble is often chemistry, not taste. Rand's metal paint tube of 1841 let painters work outdoors, but Pastoureau observes that many older landscapes now look brown because their greens have darkened and their blues faded [20]. In Seurat's *[[art:aic-27992|A Sunday on La Grande Jatte]]* the lawn is spotted with brown where chrome yellow mixed into the greens has darkened [13][20].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Not one of the 23,781 paintings in our archive holds a color within six units of this page's green over even two per cent of the canvas [80]. The nearest is an Indian painting from Kota, *Maharaja Chattarsol of Kota Shooting Lions* (1860), at just over six units across a quarter of the surface [80]. Loosen the match to twelve units and 56 paintings qualify, but 51 of them date from 1850 or later; the one that carries it most is Félix Vallotton's *[[art:cma-83462|Corn Fields]]* of 1900, with half its canvas in this green [80]. The earliest is a Japanese painting by Tawaraya Sōtatsu, *The Beach at Sumiyoshi*, from 1634 [80].

A wider test tells the same story. A clearly colored green (CIELAB chroma of 30 or more over five per cent of the canvas) appears in 125 paintings, against 2,044 for red by the same rule [80]. At a lower chroma of 15, green reaches 947 paintings, 0.8 per cent of our seventeenth-century works and 14 per cent of our twentieth-century ones [80]. That curve fits the arrival of viridian and tube paint, and also the darkening of older greens [17][20].

As photographed, the six largest colors of *A Sunday on La Grande Jatte* are greys and olives, and those of Van Gogh's *[[art:nga-163323|Green Wheat Fields, Auvers]]* are soft dull greens [80]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, the hue window is ours, and a color match is not a pigment test [80]. The swatch is a choice too: the CSS keyword `green` is the darker #008000, the American color standard calls this region strong yellowish green, and our nearest named neighbors are [[bud-green|Bud Green]] and [[shamrock-green|Shamrock Green]] [81]. In Google Books the adjective *green* is printed most in the 2010s [82].

questions.q: Why do so many old landscape paintings look brown rather than green today?
choices: Their green pigments darkened and their blues faded with age
Green paint was too expensive to use
Brown varnish was applied on purpose to imitate age
questions.answer: Their green pigments darkened and their blues faded with age

questions.q: True or false: Molière died on stage dressed in green.

choices: Red and green are opposite ends of one channel in the visual system
Red and green light cancel to black
The word does not exist in English
questions.answer: Red and green are opposite ends of one channel in the visual system
